outcome.description: Your instruments record data that will keep the Science Collective arguing for decades. The pulse pattern resolves into a repeating mathematical sequence . Not natural, not random. Encoded within it, your computer isolates what appear to be navigational coordinates, pointing to a region of space that doesn't appear on any chart you've seen. Then, as suddenly as it started, the phenomenon contracts to a point of light and goes still. Your sensor logs are the only proof it was ever there.

You edge your ship into the outer boundary of the phenomenon. Your hull vibrates at a frequency you feel in your teeth. The pulse pattern shifts . Faster, more complex . And your nav computer begins receiving data it can't parse. Raw information, flooding your systems. You pull back before the input overwhelms your processors, but the fragment you captured contains coordinates and what might be a timestamp. Something is trying very hard to tell you where to go, and when.

You reverse thrust and put fifty kilometers between you and the phenomenon. From this distance, you watch it pulse and shift for another hour before it settles into a slow, rhythmic glow. Your sensors record the pattern. Whatever it is, it seems content to wait. You file the observation and mark the coordinates. Some mysteries need more preparation before you face them.
Your instruments record exotic particle interactions that push the boundaries of known physics. The Collective would pay well for this data.
You log the coordinates and give the phenomenon a respectful berth. Some things are better left to the specialists.

You ride the gravity gradient for twenty harrowing minutes, instruments drinking in data. The readings are extraordinary . Spatial compression at a scale that shouldn't exist this far from a stellar body. The Collective will want this.
You slam the throttle and fight free of the distortion's grip. Your hull groans but holds. Behind you, the lensing effect pulses once and fades. You don't look back.

You sit in silence as the voice reads thirty-seven coordinates. Some match modern settlements. Others point to empty space . Sites that were surveyed and abandoned, or perhaps never reached at all. When the loop restarts, you notice something: the final coordinate doesn't correspond to any system on your charts. It points somewhere beyond the Expanse's mapped edge. The beacon offers no explanation. It simply begins again.

You amplify the signal and push it across local frequencies. Within minutes, other ships begin responding . Some with reverence, some with skepticism. A freighter captain transmits back: 'My grandmother used to say she could still hear the Aurelia calling.' The beacon continues its loop, indifferent to its audience.
You tag the beacon's position in your nav computer and pull away. The voice fades into static behind you, still reading its list of names to the dark.

The probe doesn't resist your scans. Its memory banks are vast and mostly intact . Geological surveys of systems the Expanse hasn't mapped yet, atmospheric data from worlds no human has visited. The manufacturing stamps are partially corroded, but you recover a partial serial number and a date: 2118. Eighty years before the Aurelia launched. Earth sent this probe during an era of expansion that history barely remembers. The question isn't who sent it. The question is what they found . And whether anyone was listening when it reported back.

You trail the probe for an hour, watching it work. It pauses at each asteroid, bathes it in scanning frequencies, logs the data, and moves on. Methodical. Patient. It has been doing this longer than anyone in the Expanse has been alive. Its projected course takes it toward the outer systems . Regions still marked 'uncharted' on your nav computer. You log the trajectory and break off. The probe continues without you, as it has for two centuries.

You alter course to give the probe space. It doesn't acknowledge your presence . It never has acknowledged anything. Just the quiet, tireless work of mapping a frontier that no one told it had already been settled. There's something admirable in that.

Hours of scanning reveal layers of complexity. The map includes eleven systems matching the known Expanse . And seven more beyond its borders, in regions no human vessel has reached. Isotope dating of the alloy returns contradictory results: some readings suggest thousands of years, others merely centuries. The engravings themselves show no tool marks your instruments can identify. The disc is either impossibly old or impossibly precise. Your data will keep scientists arguing for decades. You store the analysis alongside a single note in your log: 'We are not the first to find this place interesting.'

Seven new coordinates appear on your star charts, blinking in the margins where your maps end. You have no way to verify them . They're beyond the Expanse's explored border. But the map's known systems are accurate to within fractions of a degree. Whoever made this knew what they were doing. You file the coordinates and wonder if anyone will ever follow them. The disc continues its slow tumble as you pull away, carrying its secrets in the same patient silence that has kept them for longer than you can calculate.

You photograph every centimeter of the disc's surface and pull away without touching it. Some discoveries are bigger than one pilot and one ship. You'll submit the images to the Collective and let people smarter than you figure out what it means. But you keep one image for yourself: the cluster of dots that represents your home system, marked by hands that were never human, under stars that have been burning since before your species learned to name them.

You spend an hour carefully extracting sealed sample containers from the wreckage. Dr. Vasik catalogs each one with visible excitement . Or what passes for excitement among Axiom researchers. 'Exceptional preservation. You have contributed to a peer-reviewed study. Your name will appear in the acknowledgments section.'

You transmit your sensor readings of the debris field. Dr. Vasik accepts the data with a curt nod. 'Secondary source material. Useful for corroboration, though not a substitute for direct sampling. We will compensate you at the standard consultation rate.'

Dr. Vasik accepts your refusal with clinical detachment. 'Understood. Risk-averse behavior is statistically rational given the mortality rates in uncharted debris fields. We will source alternative assistance.' The research vessel resumes its holding pattern.

As you close range, your instruments record a cascade of data . The probe appears to be reacting to something your sensors cannot detect. Researcher Okonkwo's voice drops to a whisper: 'These readings are.. inconsistent with any known phenomenon. This will require a full review board. Your data is invaluable, Captain. We are transmitting payment and flagging your contribution as Priority One.'

Your long-range scans capture the probe's erratic behavior but lack the resolution Okonkwo hoped for. 'Peripheral data. Better than nothing, I suppose. We will need to dispatch a dedicated recovery team.' A modest payment arrives.
You leave the tumbling probe behind. On your rear sensors, it continues its strange broadcast, spinning slowly against the stars.

You fly through Nova's test field while your shields crackle and hum in unfamiliar harmonics. Your hull temperature spikes briefly . Then normalizes. Project Lead Strand is ecstatic: 'Beautiful data! The resonance cascade was within predicted parameters. Mostly. We will need to investigate that thermal anomaly, but your ship is fine. Probably run a diagnostic later. Payment is being processed . And if you experience any unusual shield behavior in the next 48 hours, do contact us.'

Strand shares the test parameters with visible reluctance. You notice the simulation was run only three times, the 'non-lethality' metric has a creative definition, and the fine print mentions 'acceptable hull micro-fracturing.' You pass. Strand shrugs: 'Your loss, Captain. Science requires bold participants.' The Nova cruiser begins scanning for the next passing ship.

Strand waves dismissively. 'Conservative risk assessment. Noted.' As you pull away, you overhear Strand on an open mic: 'Log it . Another declination. That brings our volunteer rate to.. twelve percent. Adjust the compensation package upward.'

You spend ten minutes playing sheepdog with a malfunctioning drone that seems to actively resist your efforts. Eventually you box it against a debris field and the Nova recovery shuttle snags it with a magnetic grapple. The technician sends you a payment and a weary thanks. "Third time this week. The autonomy algorithms are... ambitious."

You run a deep scan before the recovery team arrives. The drone's internal architecture is unusual . The autonomy core uses a design philosophy you've never seen in civilian tech. Nova's 'applied research' label is doing a lot of heavy lifting. You file the scan data away. Knowledge is leverage.

You adjust course to avoid the drone's erratic flight path. It bounces off another asteroid as you pass. The Nova technician sounds increasingly desperate on the recovery channel. Not your circus, not your malfunctioning prototype.

You grab the full telemetry dump before the DCMC network kills the broadcast . Twelve seconds of data that paints a picture of something that shouldn't be there. The Collective would pay well for this. The Union would want to know what DCMC found under their claims. Even the Guild might be interested. You encrypt the data and store it in your secure logs.

You relay the readings to a Union safety officer. The officer goes quiet for a long moment, then: "We've heard rumors about Omega-12 for months. This is the first hard data. I'm escalating this." The Union transfers a discretionary payment for the tip.
You let the broadcast scroll past and clear your comms buffer. Deep-core mining has always produced strange readings. Probably just instrument error. Probably.

Your sensors capture the residual energy pattern before it dissipates. The analysis is disturbing: the discharge profile doesn't match any known weapons system . Not Guild, not Union, not Collective. It's something new. Something powerful. You encrypt the data and bury it deep in your secure logs. This is the kind of information that gets people killed.

You send a concerned hail to The Fulcrum's public channel. A bored-sounding operator responds: "Routine maintenance discharge from the station's waste processing system. Nothing to be concerned about." Your instruments recorded an energy output equivalent to a capital ship's main battery, and they're calling it waste processing. You file the lie alongside the sensor data.

You don't need to be told twice . Or even once, since your computer already said it. You plot the fastest course out of The Fulcrum's sensor range and don't look back. The shockwave echoes in your hull for minutes after you've cleared the sector. Whatever they're building in there, you want no part of it.
